{{Short description|Special functions used to build correlation functions in 2D CFTs}}
In [[two-dimensional conformal field theory]], '''Virasoro conformal blocks''' (named after [[Miguel Ángel Virasoro (physicist)|Miguel Ángel Virasoro]]) are [[special functions]] that serve as building blocks of [[correlation function (quantum field theory)|correlation functions]]. On a given punctured [[Riemann surface]], Virasoro conformal blocks form a particular basis of the space of solutions of the [[Two-dimensional conformal field theory#Conformal Ward identities|conformal Ward identities]]. Zero-point blocks on the torus are [[character theory|characters]] of representations of the [[Virasoro algebra]]; four-point blocks on the sphere reduce to [[hypergeometric function]]s in special cases, but are in general much more complicated. In two dimensions as in other dimensions, conformal blocks play an essential role in the [[conformal bootstrap]] approach to [[conformal field theory]].

== Definition ==

=== Definition from OPEs ===

Using [[operator product expansion]]s (OPEs), 
an <math>N</math>-point function on the sphere can be written as a combination of three-point structure constants, and universal quantities called '''<math>N</math>-point conformal blocks'''.<ref name="BYB">P. Di Francesco, P. Mathieu, and D. Sénéchal, ''Conformal Field Theory'', 1997, {{ISBN|0-387-94785-X}}</ref><ref name="rib14" />

Given an <math>N</math>-point function, 
there are several types of conformal blocks, depending on which OPEs are used. In the case <math>N=4</math>, there are three types of conformal blocks, corresponding to three possible decompositions of the same four-point function. Schematically, these decompositions read
:<math>\left\langle V_1V_2V_3V_4\right\rangle
=\sum_s C_{12s}C_{s34}\mathcal{F}^{\text{(s-channel)}}_s = \sum_t C_{14t}C_{t23}\mathcal{F}^{\text{(t-channel)}}_t = \sum_u C_{13u}C_{24u}\mathcal{F}^{\text{(u-channel)}}_u\ ,
</math>
where <math>C</math> are structure constants and <math>\mathcal{F}</math> are conformal blocks. The sums are over representations of the conformal algebra that appear in the CFT's spectrum. OPEs involve sums over the spectrum, i.e. over representations and over states in representations, but the sums over states are absorbed in the conformal blocks.

In two dimensions, the symmetry algebra factorizes into two copies of the Virasoro algebra, called left-moving and right-moving. If the fields are factorized too, then the conformal blocks factorize as well, and the factors are called '''Virasoro conformal blocks'''. Left-moving Virasoro conformal blocks are locally holomorphic functions of the fields' positions <math>z_i</math>; right-moving Virasoro conformal blocks are the same functions of <math>\bar z_i</math>. The factorization of a conformal block into Virasoro conformal blocks is of the type
:<math> \mathcal{F}^{\text{(s-channel)}}_{s_L\otimes s_R}(\{z_i\}) = \mathcal{F}^{\text{(s-channel, Virasoro)}}_{s_L}(\{z_i\})\mathcal{F}^{\text{(s-channel, Virasoro)}}_{s_R}(\{\bar z_i\})\ ,
</math>
where <math>s_L,s_R</math> are representations of the left- and right-moving Virasoro algebras respectively.

=== Definition from Virasoro Ward identities ===

[[Two-dimensional conformal field theory#Conformal Ward identities|Conformal Ward identities]] are the linear equations that correlation functions obey, as a result of [[conformal symmetry]].

In two dimensions, conformal Ward identities decompose into left-moving and right-moving Virasoro Ward identities. '''Virasoro conformal blocks''' are solutions of the Virasoro Ward identities.<ref name="MS"/><ref>{{Cite arXiv |eprint = 1708.00680|last1 = Teschner|first1 = Joerg|title = A guide to two-dimensional conformal field theory|year = 2017|class = hep-th}}</ref>

OPEs define specific bases of Virasoro conformal blocks, such as the s-channel basis in the case of four-point blocks. The blocks that are defined from OPEs are special cases of the blocks that are defined from Ward identities.

== Properties ==

Any linear holomorphic equation that is obeyed by a correlation function, must also hold for the corresponding conformal blocks. In addition, specific bases of conformal blocks come with extra properties that are not inherited from the correlation function.

Conformal blocks that involve only [[Two-dimensional conformal field theory#State-field correspondence|primary fields]] have relatively simple properties. Conformal blocks that involve descendant fields can then be deduced using local [[Two-dimensional conformal field theory#Conformal Ward identities|Ward identities]]. An s-channel four-point block of primary fields depends on the four fields' conformal dimensions <math>\Delta_i,</math> on their positions <math>z_i,</math> and on the s-channel conformal dimension <math>\Delta_s</math>. It can be written as <math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\Delta_i|\{z_i\}),</math> where the dependence on the [[Virasoro algebra]]'s [[central charge]] is kept implicit.

=== Conformal covariance ===

In an <math>N</math>-point block on the sphere, Ward identities for global conformal symmetry reduce the dependence on the <math>N</math> field positions to a dependence on <math>N-3</math> [[cross-ratio]]s. In the case <math>N=4,</math>

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_i\}|\{z_i\})= z_{23}^{\Delta_1-\Delta_2-\Delta_3+\Delta_4} z_{13}^{-2\Delta_1} z_{34}^{\Delta_1+\Delta_2-\Delta_3-\Delta_4} z_{24}^{-\Delta_1-\Delta_2+\Delta_3-\Delta_4}\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s} (\{\Delta_i \}|z),</math>

where <math>z_{ij}=z_i-z_j,</math> and

:<math>z= \frac{z_{12}z_{34}}{z_{13}z_{24}}</math>

is the cross-ratio, and the reduced block <math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_i\}|z)</math> coincides with the original block where three positions are sent to <math>(0,\infty, 1),</math>

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_i\}|z)= \mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_i\}|z,0,\infty,1).</math>

=== Singularities in the fields' positions===

Like correlation functions, conformal blocks are singular when two fields coincide. Unlike correlation functions, conformal blocks have very simple behaviours at some of these singularities. As a consequence of their definition from OPEs, s-channel four-point blocks obey

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_i\}|z) \underset{z\to 0}{=} z^{\Delta_s-\Delta_1-\Delta_2}\left\{1 + \sum_{N=1}^\infty c_N z^N\right\}\ ,</math>

for some coefficients <math>c_N</math>. On the other hand, s-channel blocks have complicated singular behaviours at <math>z=1,\infty</math>: it is t-channel blocks that are simple at <math>z=1</math>, and u-channel blocks that are simple at <math>z=\infty.</math>

In a four-point block that obeys a [[Two-dimensional conformal field theory#BPZ equations|BPZ differential equation]], <math>z=0,1,\infty</math> are [[regular singular point]]s of the differential equation, and <math>\Delta_s-\Delta_1-\Delta_2</math> is a characteristic exponent of the differential equation. For a differential equation of order <math>n</math>, the <math>n</math> characteristic exponents correspond to the <math>n</math> values of <math>\Delta_s</math> that are allowed by the [[fusion rules]].

=== Field permutations ===

Permutations of the fields <math>V_i(z_i)</math> leave the correlation function

:<math>\left\langle\prod_{i=1}^NV_i(z_i)\right\rangle</math>

invariant, and therefore relate different bases of conformal blocks with one another. In the case of four-point blocks, t-channel blocks are related to s-channel blocks by<ref name="rib14" />

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{\Delta}(\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3,\Delta_4|z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4) = \mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta}(\Delta_1, \Delta_4, \Delta_3,\Delta_2|z_1,z_4,z_3,z_2),</math>

or equivalently

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{\Delta}(\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3,\Delta_4|z) = \mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta} (\Delta_1, \Delta_4, \Delta_3, \Delta_2| 1-z).</math>

=== Fusing matrix ===

The change of bases from s-channel to t-channel four-point blocks is characterized by the '''fusing matrix''' (or fusion kernel) <math>F</math>, such that

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_i\}|\{z_i\}) 
= \int_{i\mathbb{R}} dP_t\ F_{\Delta_s,\Delta_t}\begin{bmatrix} \Delta_2 & \Delta_3 \\ \Delta_1 & \Delta_4 \end{bmatrix} \mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{\Delta_t}(\{\Delta_i\}|\{z_i\}).</math>

The fusing matrix is a function of the central charge and conformal dimensions, but it does not depend on the positions <math>z_i.</math> The momentum <math>P_t</math> is defined in terms of the dimension <math>\Delta_t</math> by

:<math> \Delta = \frac{c-1}{24}-P^2.</math>

The values <math>P\in i\mathbb{R}</math> correspond to the spectrum of [[Liouville field theory|Liouville theory]]. In <math>N</math>-point blocks on the sphere, the change of bases between two sets of blocks that are defined from different sequences of OPEs can always be written in terms of the fusing matrix, and a simple matrix that describes the permutation of the first two fields in an s-channel block,<ref name="MS"/>

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3,\Delta_4|z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4) = e^{i\pi(\Delta_s-\Delta_1-\Delta_2)} \mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\Delta_2,\Delta_1,\Delta_3,\Delta_4|z_2,z_1,z_3,z_4).</math>

The expression of the fusing matrix depends on the value of the central charge <math>c</math>, equivalently on the parameter <math>b</math> defined by

:<math> c= 1+6Q^2, \qquad Q=b+b^{-1}. </math>

The special case <math> c\leq 1 </math> gives rise to different expressions depending on <math>b^2\in\mathbb{Q}</math><ref name="rt25" /> or <math>b^2\in \mathbb{R}_{<0}\backslash\mathbb{Q}_{<0}</math>.<ref name="rou24"/> In the general case <math> c\in \mathbb{C}\backslash (-\infty, 1]</math> with <math>P_i\in i\R</math>, the fusing matrix is<ref>{{Cite arXiv |eprint = 1202.4698|last1 = Teschner|first1 = J.|last2 = Vartanov|first2 = G. S.|title = 6j symbols for the modular double, quantum hyperbolic geometry, and supersymmetric gauge theories|year = 2012|class = hep-th}}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}
F_{\Delta_s,\Delta_t} &\begin{bmatrix} \Delta_2 & \Delta_3 \\ \Delta_1 & \Delta_4 \end{bmatrix} = \\
&= \left(\prod_{\pm}\frac{\Gamma_b(Q\pm 2P_s)}{\Gamma_b(\pm 2P_t)}\right) \frac{\Xi_+(P_1,P_4,P_t)\Xi_+(P_2,P_3,P_t)}{\Xi_-(P_1,P_2,P_s)\Xi_-(P_3,P_4,P_s)} \times 
\\
&\quad \times \int_{\frac{Q}{4}+i\R}du \ S_b \left (u-P_{12s} \right ) S_b \left (u-P_{s34} \right ) S_b \left (u-P_{23t} \right )S_b \left (u-P_{t14} \right )
\\ 
& \qquad \times 
S_b \left ( \tfrac{Q}{2}-u+P_{1234} \right ) S_b \left (\tfrac{Q}{2}-u+P_{st13} \right ) S_b \left(\tfrac{Q}{2}-u+P_{st24} \right)S_b \left(\tfrac{Q}{2}-u \right )
\end{align}</math>

where <math>\Gamma_b</math> is a [[double gamma function]],

:<math>\begin{align}
S_b(x)  &= \frac{\Gamma_b(x)}{\Gamma_b(Q-x)} \\[6pt]
\Xi_\epsilon(P_1,P_2,P_3) &=\prod_{\underset{\epsilon_1\epsilon_2\epsilon_3=\epsilon}{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3=\pm }} \Gamma_b\left(\tfrac{Q}{2}+\sum_i\epsilon_iP_i\right) \\[6pt]
P_{ijk} &= P_i+P_j+P_k
\end{align}</math>

Although its expression is simpler in terms of momentums <math>P_i</math> than in terms of conformal dimensions <math>\Delta_i</math>, the fusing matrix is really a function of <math>\Delta_i</math>, i.e. a function of <math>P_i</math> that is invariant under <math>P_i\to -P_i</math>. In the expression for the fusing matrix, the integral is a '''hyperbolic Barnes integral'''. Up to normalization, the fusing matrix coincides with '''Ruijsenaars' hypergeometric function''', with the arguments <math>P_s,P_t</math> and parameters <math>b,b^{-1},P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4</math>.<ref name="Roussillon 2020"/> The fusing matrix has several different integral representations, and obeys many nontrivial identities.<ref name="ebe23"/>

=== Exponentiation at large central charge ===

In the large central charge limit with fixed ratios <math>\tfrac{\Delta_i}{c}</math> (including for channel dimensions), the logarithm of a conformal block is linear in <math>c</math>. In the case of a sphere 4-point block, this means<ref name="gh26"/>
:<math>
\log \mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3,\Delta_4\}|z)\ \underset{c\to \infty}{=} \ c\cdot f^{(s)}_{\frac{\Delta_s}{c}}\left(\left\{\tfrac{\Delta_1}{c},\tfrac{\Delta_2}{c},\tfrac{\Delta_3}{c},\tfrac{\Delta_4}{c}\right\}\Big|z\right) + O(1)
</math>
This property underlies Zamolodchikov's recursive representation.

=== Triality of sphere 4-point blocks ===

Up to simple prefactors of the type <math>z^\alpha (1-z)^\beta</math>, 4-point sphere conformal blocks are invariant under<ref name="kl25"/> 
:<math>
(P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4) \to \frac12(P_1+P_2+P_3+P_4,P_1+P_2-P_3-P_4,P_1-P_2+P_3-P_4,P_1-P_2-P_3+P_4)
</math>

== Computation of conformal blocks ==

=== From the definition ===

The definition from OPEs leads to an expression for an s-channel four-point conformal block as a sum over states in the s-channel representation, of the type<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=0907.3946|last1=Marshakov|first1=A.|last2=Mironov|first2=A.|last3=Morozov|first3=A.|title=On Combinatorial Expansions of Conformal Blocks|journal=Theoretical and Mathematical Physics|year=2009|volume=164|pages=831–852|doi=10.1007/s11232-010-0067-6|s2cid=16017224}}</ref> 
:<math> \mathcal{F}^{\text{(s)}}_{\Delta_s}(\{\Delta_i\}|z)= z^{\Delta_s-\Delta_1-\Delta_2} \left\{1+\sum_{N=1}^\infty c_N z^N\right\} \quad \text{with} \quad c_N = 
\sum_{|L|=|L'|=N} f_{12s}^L Q_{L,L'}^s f_{43s}^{L'}\ .
</math>
The sum is over creation modes <math>L,L'</math> of the [[Virasoro algebra]], i.e. combinations of the type <math> L=\prod_i L_{-n_i}</math> of Virasoro generators with <math>1\leq n_1\leq n_2\leq \cdots</math>, whose level is <math>|L|=\sum n_i</math>. Such generators correspond to basis states in the Verma module with the conformal dimension <math>\Delta_s</math>. 
The coefficient <math>f_{12s}^L</math> is a function of <math>\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_s,L</math>, which is known explicitly. The quantity <math>Q_{L,L'}^s</math> is a matrix element of the inverse [[Virasoro algebra#Shapovalov form|Shapovalov form]]: it is a function of <math>c,\Delta_s,L,L'</math> which vanishes if <math>|L|\neq |L'|</math>, and diverges for <math>|L|=N</math> if there is a null vector at level <math>N</math>.
The first nontrivial coefficient is 
:<math>
c_1=\frac{(\Delta_s+\Delta_1-\Delta_2)(\Delta_s+\Delta_4-\Delta_3)}{2\Delta_s}\ . 
</math>
(In particular, <math>Q_{L_{-1},L_{-1}}^s=\frac{1}{2\Delta_s}</math> does not depend on the central charge <math>c</math>.)
An explicit expression for <math>c_N</math> is known.<ref name="fqs25"/>

=== Zamolodchikov's recursive representation ===

In [[Alexei Zamolodchikov]]'s recursive representation of four-point blocks on the sphere, the cross-ratio <math>z</math> appears via the [[nome (mathematics)|nome]] 
:<math>
q = \exp -\pi \frac{F(\frac12,\frac12,1,1-z)}{F(\frac12,\frac12,1,z)} \underset{z\to 0}{=} \frac{z}{16}+\frac{z^2}{32}+O(z^3)  \quad \iff \quad z = \frac{\theta_2(q)^4}{\theta_3(q)^4} \underset{q\to 0}{=} 16 q - 128 q^2 + O(q^3)
</math> 
where <math>F</math> is the [[hypergeometric function]], and we introduce the Jacobi [[theta function]]s 
:<math>
\theta_2(q) =  2q^\frac14\sum_{n=0}^\infty q^{n(n+1)} \quad , \quad \theta_3(q) = \sum_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}} q^{n^2}\quad , \quad \theta_4(q) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty (-1)^n q^{n^2}
</math>
The representation is of the type<ref name=rib24/>
:<math>
\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{\Delta}(\{\Delta_i\}|z) = (16q)^{\Delta -\frac{Q^2}{4}} \left[\prod_{k=2,3,4}\left(\theta_k(q)^{-4}\right)^{\Delta_k-\frac{Q^2}{4}+(-1)^k\Delta_1}\right] H_{\Delta}(\{\Delta_i\}|q)\ .
</math>
The function <math>H_{\Delta}(\{\Delta_i\}|q)</math> is a [[power series]] in <math>q</math>, which is recursively defined by 
:<math>
H_{\Delta}(\{\Delta_i\}|q) = 1 + \sum_{m,n=1}^\infty \frac{(16q)^{mn}}{\Delta-\Delta_{(m,n)}} R_{m,n} H_{\Delta_{(m,-n)}}(\{\Delta_i\}|q)\ .
</math>
In this formula, the positions <math>\Delta_{(m,n)}</math> of the poles are the dimensions of degenerate representations, which correspond to the momentums
:<math>
P_{(m,n)} = \frac12 \left(mb+nb^{-1}\right)\ .
</math>
The residues <math>R_{m,n}</math> are given by 
:<math>
 R_{m,n} = \frac{2P_{( 0,0)} P_{( m,n)}}{\prod_{r=1-m}^m \prod_{s=1-n}^n 2P_{(r,s)}}
\prod_{r\overset{2}{=}1-m}^{m-1} \prod_{s\overset{2}{=}1-n}^{n-1} \prod_\pm (P_2\pm P_1 + P_{( r,s)}) (P_3\pm P_4 +P_{( r,s)})\ ,
</math>
where the superscript in <math>\overset{2}{=}</math> indicates a product that runs by increments of <math>2</math>. The recursion relation for <math>H_{\Delta}(\{\Delta_i\}|q)</math> can be solved, giving rise to an explicit (but impractical) formula.<ref name="rib14">{{cite arXiv |eprint=1406.4290|last1=Ribault|first1=Sylvain|title=Conformal field theory on the plane|class=hep-th|year=2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=1502.07742|last1=Perlmutter|first1=Eric|title=Virasoro conformal blocks in closed form|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics|year=2015|volume=2015|issue=8|article-number=88|doi=10.1007/JHEP08(2015)088|bibcode=2015JHEP...08..088P|s2cid=54075672}}</ref>

While the coefficients of the power series <math>H_{\Delta}(\{\Delta_i\}|q)</math> need not be positive in [[unitarity (physics)|unitary]] theories, the coefficients of <math>\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1-q^{2k})^{-\frac12} H_{\Delta}(\{\Delta_i\}|q)</math> are positive, due to this combination's interpretation in terms of sums of states in the pillow geometry. And the block's prefactors can be interpreted in terms of the conformal transformation from the sphere to the pillow.<ref name="msz15"/>

The recursive representation can be seen as an expansion around <math>\Delta=\infty</math>. It is sometimes called the '''<math>\Delta</math>-recursion''', in order to distinguish it from the '''<math>c</math>-recursion''': another recursive representation, also due to [[Alexei Zamolodchikov]], which expands around <math>c=\infty</math>, and generates a series in powers of <math>z</math>.
The <math>c</math>-recursion can be generalized to <math>N</math>-point Virasoro conformal blocks on arbitrary [[Riemann surface]]s.<ref name="ccy17"/> The <math>\Delta</math>-recursion can be generalized to [[#One-point blocks on the torus|one-point blocks on the torus]]. In other cases, there are no known generalizations of the <math>\Delta</math>-recursion, but there exist modified <math>c</math>-recursions that generate series in powers of <math>z</math>.<ref name="ccy17"/>

=== From the AGT relation to instanton counting  ===

The Alday–Gaiotto–Tachikawa relation between two-dimensional conformal field theory  and [[supersymmetric gauge theory]], more specifically, between the conformal blocks of Liouville theory and Nekrasov partition functions<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = hep-th/0206161|doi = 10.4310/ATMP.2003.v7.n5.a4|title = Seiberg-Witten Prepotential from Instanton Counting|year = 2004|last1 = Nekrasov|first1 = Nikita|journal = Advances in Theoretical and Mathematical Physics|volume = 7|number = 5|pages = 831–864|s2cid = 2285041}}</ref> of supersymmetric gauge theories in four dimensions, leads to combinatorial expressions for conformal blocks as sums over [[Young diagram]]s. Each diagram can be interpreted as a state in a representation of the Virasoro algebra, times an abelian [[affine Lie algebra]].<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1012.1312|doi = 10.1007/s11005-011-0503-z|title = On Combinatorial Expansion of the Conformal Blocks Arising from AGT Conjecture|year = 2011|last1 = Alba|first1 = Vasyl A.|last2 = Fateev|first2 = Vladimir A.|last3 = Litvinov|first3 = Alexey V.|last4 = Tarnopolskiy|first4 = Grigory M.|journal = Letters in Mathematical Physics|volume = 98|issue = 1|pages = 33–64|bibcode = 2011LMaPh..98...33A|s2cid = 119143670}}</ref>

== Special cases ==

=== Zero-point blocks on the torus ===
A zero-point block does not depend on field positions, but it depends on the [[Moduli of algebraic curves|moduli]] of the underlying [[Riemann surface]]. In the case of the torus

:<math>\frac{\Complex}{\Z+\tau\Z},</math>

that dependence is better written through <math>q=e^{2\pi i\tau}</math> and the zero-point block associated to a representation <math>\mathcal{R}</math> of the [[Virasoro algebra]] is

:<math>\chi_\mathcal{R}(\tau) = \operatorname{Tr}_\mathcal{R} q^{L_0-\frac{c}{24}},</math>

where <math>L_0</math> is a generator of the Virasoro algebra. This coincides with the [[character theory|character]] of <math>\mathcal{R}.</math> The characters of some highest-weight representations are:<ref name="BYB"/>

* [[Virasoro algebra#Lowest weight representations|Verma module]] with conformal dimension <math>\Delta=\tfrac{c-1}{24}-P^2</math>:
::<math> \chi_P(\tau) = \frac{q^{-P^2}}{\eta(\tau)},</math> 
:where <math>\eta(\tau)</math> is the [[Dedekind eta function]].

* Degenerate representation with the momentum <math>P_{(r,s)} </math>:
::<math> \chi_{(r,s)}(\tau) = \chi_{P_{(r,s)}}(\tau) - \chi_{P_{(r,-s)}}(\tau).</math>

* Fully degenerate representation at rational <math>b^2 = -\tfrac{p}{q}</math>:
::<math>\chi_{(r,s)}(\tau) = \sum_{k\in\Z} \left(\chi_{P_{(r,s)}+ik\sqrt{pq}}(\tau) - \chi_{P_{(r,-s)}+ik\sqrt{pq}}(\tau) \right). </math>

The characters transform linearly under the [[modular group|modular transformations]]:

:<math>\tau \to \frac{a\tau + b}{c\tau +d}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in SL_2(\Z).</math>

In particular their transformation under <math>\tau \to -\tfrac{1}{\tau}</math> is described by the '''modular S-matrix'''. Using the S-matrix, constraints on a CFT's spectrum can be derived from the [[modular invariance]] of the torus partition function, leading in particular to the [[ADE classification]] of [[Minimal model (physics)|minimal models]].<ref>A. Cappelli, J-B. Zuber, "A-D-E Classification of Conformal Field Theories", [http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/A-D-E_Classification_of_Conformal_Field_Theories Scholarpedia]</ref> These are related to the [[modular group representation]]s of [[Modular tensor category|modular tensor categories]].

=== One-point blocks on the torus ===

An arbitrary one-point block on the torus can be written in terms of a four-point block on the sphere at a different central charge. This relation maps the modulus of the torus to the cross-ratio of the four points' positions, and three of the four fields on the sphere have the fixed momentum <math>P_{(0,\frac12)} = \tfrac{1}{4b}</math>:<ref name="flno09"/><ref name="hjs09"/>
:<math>
H^\text{torus}_{P'}(P_1|q^2) = H_{P}\left(\left.\tfrac{1}{4b},P_2,\tfrac{1}{4b},\tfrac{1}{4b}\right|q\right)  \quad \text{with}\quad \left\{\begin{array}{l} b=\frac{b'}{\sqrt{2}}\\ P_2=\frac{P_1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ P=\sqrt{2}P' \end{array}\right.
</math>
where 
* <math>H_{P_s}\left(\left.P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4\right|q\right)</math> is the non-trivial factor of the sphere four-point block in Zamolodchikov's recursive representation, written in terms of momentums <math>P_i</math> instead of dimensions <math>\Delta_i</math>.
* <math>H^\text{torus}_{P}(P_1|q)</math> is the non-trivial factor of the torus one-point block <math>\mathcal{F}^\text{torus}_{\Delta}(\Delta_1|q) = q^{\Delta-\frac{c-1}{24}}\eta(q)^{-1}H^\text{torus}_{\Delta}(\Delta_1|q)</math>, where <math>\eta(q)</math> is the [[Dedekind eta function]], the modular parameter <math>\tau</math> of the torus is such that <math>q=e^{2\pi i\tau}</math>, and the field on the torus has the dimension <math>\Delta_1</math>.

The recursive representation of one-point blocks on the torus is<ref name="fl09"/>
:<math>H^\text{torus}_{\Delta}(\Delta_1|q) = 1 + \sum_{m,n=1}^\infty \frac{q^{mn}}{\Delta-\Delta_{(m,n)}} R^\text{torus}_{m,n} H^\text{torus}_{\Delta_{(m,-n)}}(\Delta_1|q)\ ,
</math>
where the residues are 
:<math>
R^\text{torus}_{m,n} = \frac{2P_{( 0,0)} P_{( m,n)}}{\prod_{r=1-m}^m \prod_{s=1-n}^n 2P_{(r,s)}}
\prod_{r\overset{2}{=}1-2m}^{2m-1} \prod_{s\overset{2}{=}1-2n}^{2n-1} \left(P_1+P_{(r,s)}\right)\ .
</math>
Under modular transformations, one-point blocks on the torus behave as 
:<math>
\mathcal{F}^\text{torus}_{P}\left(P_1|-\tfrac{1}{\tau}\right) = \int_{i\mathbb{R}} dP'\ S_{P,P'}(P_1)\mathcal{F}^\text{torus}_{P'}\left(P_1|\tau\right)\ ,
</math>
where the '''modular kernel''' is<ref name="tes03"/><ref name="nem15"/>
:<math>
S_{P,P'}(P_1) =  \frac{\sqrt{2}}{S_b(\frac{Q}{2}+P_1)}
\prod_\pm \frac{\Gamma_b(Q\pm 2P)}{\Gamma_b(\pm 2P')} \frac{\Gamma_b(\frac{Q}{2}-P_1\pm 2P')}{\Gamma_b(\frac{Q}{2}-P_1\pm 2P)} \int_{i\mathbb{R}} \frac{du}{i}\ e^{4\pi iPu} \prod_{\pm,\pm} S_b\left(\tfrac{Q}{4}+\tfrac{P_1}{2} \pm u\pm P'\right)\ .
</math>

=== Hypergeometric blocks ===

For a four-point function on the sphere

:<math>\left\langle V_{\langle 2,1 \rangle}(x)\prod_{i=1}^3 V_{\Delta_i}(z_i)\right\rangle </math>

where one field has a null vector at level two, the second-order [[Two-dimensional conformal field theory#BPZ equations|BPZ equation]] reduces to the hypergeometric equation. A basis of solutions is made of the two s-channel conformal blocks that are allowed by the [[fusion rules]], and these blocks can be written in terms of the [[hypergeometric function]],

:<math>
\begin{align}
\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{P_1+\epsilon\frac{b}{2}}(z) 
&= z^{\frac12+\frac{b^2}{2}+b\epsilon P_1} (1-z)^{\frac12+\frac{b^2}{2}+bP_3} 
\\ &\times
F\left(\tfrac12 + b(\epsilon P_1+P_2+P_3),\tfrac12 + b(\epsilon P_1-P_2+P_3),1 + 2b\epsilon P_1,z\right),
\end{align}
</math>

with <math>\epsilon\in\{+,-\}.</math> Another basis is made of the two t-channel conformal blocks,

:<math>
\begin{align}
\mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{P_3+\epsilon\frac{b}{2}}(z) 
&= z^{\frac12+\frac{b^2}{2}+b P_1} (1-z)^{\frac12+\frac{b^2}{2}+b\epsilon P_3} 
\\ &\times 
F\left(\tfrac12 + b( P_1+P_2+\epsilon P_3),\tfrac12 + b(P_1-P_2+\epsilon P_3), 1 + 2b\epsilon P_3,1-z\right).
\end{align}
</math>

The fusing matrix is the  matrix of size two such that

:<math>\mathcal{F}^{(s)}_{P_1+\epsilon_1\frac{b}{2}}(x) = \sum_{\epsilon_3=\pm} F_{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_3} \mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{P_3+\epsilon_3\frac{b}{2}}(x), </math>

whose explicit expression is

:<math> F_{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_3} = \frac{\Gamma(1-2b\epsilon_1P_1)\Gamma(2b\epsilon_3P_3)}{\prod_\pm \Gamma(\frac12+b(-\epsilon_1P_1\pm P_2+\epsilon_3P_3))}. </math>

Hypergeometric conformal blocks play an important role in the analytic bootstrap approach to two-dimensional CFT.<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=hep-th/9507109|last1=Teschner|first1=Joerg.|title=On the Liouville three-point function|journal=Physics Letters B|year=1995|volume=363|issue=1–2|pages=65–70|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(95)01200-A|bibcode=1995PhLB..363...65T|s2cid=15910029}}</ref><ref name=rib24/>

=== Solutions of the Painlevé VI equation ===

If <math> c=1,</math> then certain linear combinations of s-channel conformal blocks are solutions of the [[Painlevé transcendents|Painlevé VI nonlinear differential equation]].<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1207.0787|doi = 10.1007/JHEP10(2012)038|title = Conformal field theory of Painlevé VI|year = 2012|last1 = Gamayun|first1 = O.|last2 = Iorgov|first2 = N.|last3 = Lisovyy|first3 = O.|journal = Journal of High Energy Physics|volume = 2012|issue = 10|page = 038|bibcode = 2012JHEP...10..038G|s2cid = 119610935}}</ref> The relevant linear combinations involve sums over sets of momentums of the type <math>P_s+i\Z.</math> This allows conformal blocks to be deduced from solutions of the Painlevé VI equation and vice versa. This also leads to a relatively simple formula for the fusing matrix at <math>c=1.</math><ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1308.4092|doi = 10.1007/JHEP12(2013)029|title = Painlevé VI connection problem and monodromy of c = 1 conformal blocks|year = 2013|last1 = Iorgov|first1 = N.|last2 = Lisovyy|first2 = O.|last3 = Tykhyy|first3 = Yu.|journal = Journal of High Energy Physics|volume = 2013|issue = 12|page = 029|bibcode = 2013JHEP...12..029I|s2cid = 56401903}}</ref> Curiously, the <math>c=\infty</math> limit of conformal blocks is also related to the Painlevé VI equation.<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1309.4700|doi = 10.1007/JHEP07(2014)144|title = Classical conformal blocks and Painlevé VI|year = 2014|last1 = Litvinov|first1 = Alexey|last2 = Lukyanov|first2 = Sergei|last3 = Nekrasov|first3 = Nikita|last4 = Zamolodchikov|first4 = Alexander|journal = Journal of High Energy Physics|volume = 2014|issue = 7|page = 144|bibcode = 2014JHEP...07..144L|s2cid = 119710593}}</ref> The relation between the <math>c=\infty</math> and the <math>c=1</math> limits, mysterious on the conformal field theory side, is explained naturally in the context of four dimensional gauge theories, using blowup equations,<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 2007.03646|title =  Blowups in BPS/CFT correspondence, and Painlevé VI|year = 2020|last1 = Nekrasov|first1 = Nikita| journal = Annales Henri Poincaré| volume=25 | pages=1123–1213 |doi = 10.1007/s00023-023-01301-5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 2007.03660
|doi = 10.1007/JHEP12(2020)006|title = Riemann-Hilbert correspondence and blown up surface defects
|year = 2020|last1 = Jeong|first1 = Saebyeok|last2 = Nekrasov|first2 = Nikita|journal = Journal of High Energy Physics|volume = 2020|issue = 12|page = 006|bibcode = 2020JHEP...12..006J|s2cid = 220381427}}</ref> and can be generalized to more general pairs <math>c, c'</math>of central charges.

== Generalizations ==

=== Other representations of the Virasoro algebra ===

The Virasoro conformal blocks that are described in this article are associated to a certain type of representations of the Virasoro algebra: highest-weight representations, in other words Verma modules and their cosets.<ref name="rib14" /> Correlation functions that involve other types of representations give rise to other types of conformal blocks. For example:
* [[Logarithmic conformal field theory]] involves representations where the Virasoro generator <math>L_0</math> is not diagonalizable, which give rise to blocks that depend logarithmically on field positions. 
* Representations can be built from states on which some annihilation modes of the Virasoro algebra act diagonally, rather than vanishing. The corresponding conformal blocks have been called '''irregular conformal blocks'''.<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1203.1052|doi = 10.1007/JHEP12(2012)050|title = Irregular singularities in Liouville theory and Argyres-Douglas type gauge theories|year = 2012|last1 = Gaiotto|first1 = D.|last2 = Teschner|first2 = J.|journal = Journal of High Energy Physics|volume = 2012|issue = 12|page = 50|bibcode = 2012JHEP...12..050G|s2cid = 118380071}}</ref>

=== Larger symmetry algebras ===
In a theory whose symmetry algebra is larger than the Virasoro algebra, for example a [[WZW model]] or a theory with [[W-symmetry]], correlation functions can in principle be decomposed into Virasoro conformal blocks, but that decomposition typically involves too many terms to be useful. Instead, it is possible to use conformal blocks based on the larger algebra: for example, in a WZW model, conformal blocks based on the corresponding [[affine Lie algebra]], which obey [[Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations]].
